about: Every correction the Lists page applies on top of the generated data (lists.json, author_items.json, citations.csv, list_checks.csv). tools/lists.py applies them at build time, so a data regeneration cannot undo one silently: each entry names the value it expects to find and the build stops if the data holds neither that value nor the corrected one. Dates and reasons come from the retraction notices, never from the Retraction Watch database.

A notice with no stated reason, or an unclear one, still counts and is marked reason unclear. Applied where we have read the notice.

Then come our response with the facts (our_response) and the changes made to the entry since our letter (changes), whether the reply prompted them or a rule applied to every entry did. No reply is left out, and no one is asked for permission to be quoted. Contact details and third-party personal data are removed from anything printed. Acknowledgements and automatic replies are not replies. tools/lists.py stops the build if a reply has no quote, a quote over 40 words, a printed field holding an email address or phone number, names an entry that is not on the lists or among the excluded works, or if the entry's counts no longer match entry_now. replies.summary: Dr Sahebkar says a retraction is not a single verdict on a paper: notices range from fabricated data to duplicate publication, authorship disputes or a problem in one figure unrelated to the result being cited, and COPE guidance recommends citing retracted work with its status clearly marked. All seven papers in our letter are reviews of hundreds of sources, and he says none of their conclusions depends on the retracted papers. He asks that authors be compared by rates normalised by their total publications and cited references, not ranked by absolute counts, since a ranking by count is led by the authors who publish most. replies.statement:
Thank you for contacting me before publication and providing an opportunity to respond. I take the accuracy of the scientific record seriously.

I have checked the identified references and their surrounding passages. I acknowledge that the listed studies have retraction notices and are cited in support of scientific statements in the reviews. However, this does not, by itself, establish prior awareness of the retractions, individual misconduct, or that the reviews’ overall conclusions are invalid.

The publication timeline requires context. The oxaliplatin review was submitted on 21 September 2023, before the cited circPTK2 study was retracted on 18 October 2023, although the review was revised and published afterward. Please reflect this distinction in your account.

It is also important to distinguish the status of a review from that of a study it cites. For example, the May 2022 correction to “The long and short non-coding RNAs modulating EZH2 signaling in cancer” concerned a co-author’s name; it was not a retraction of that review. I recognise that this correction does not resolve the separate issue of its cited sources.

Regarding prior awareness, I would need to review the manuscript history and relevant correspondence before providing an accurate account for each citation. Assessing the effect on the reviews’ conclusions likewise requires examining the particular claims and the remaining evidence. Citation counts alone cannot establish that an entire review is unreliable. I remain willing to work with the co-authors and journals to assess the affected statements and pursue appropriate corrections.

I also have concerns about the opportunity afforded to authors to respond to editorial decisions. In some instances involving our own papers, my understanding is that we were notified only after retraction and were not given a meaningful opportunity to respond beforehand. This is a separate concern from the status of the studies cited in those papers.

Regarding the separate Elsevier retraction matter, I continue to disagree strongly with the decision and dispute the grounds provided. In our correspondence with Elsevier, we explained our position that the identified reference mismatches and Table 3 error could be addressed through a formal correction without invalidating the review’s overall conclusions. We supplied proposed corrections and requested a specific explanation of why a correction was considered insufficient. In our view, those concerns were not adequately addressed.

Please distinguish this disputed editorial matter from your citation analysis. If you discuss it, please accurately record that the authors disagree with the retraction and dispute its grounds.

I appreciate your clarification that your analysis concerns citation use rather than intent. Please preserve that distinction in the published presentation. As your figures remain provisional and human verification is pending, please provide the completed human-review findings when available. I request that publication of my individual entry be deferred until I have had a reasonable opportunity to review and respond to those findings.

I would welcome publication of this response alongside any summary concerning me, so that readers can consider my position in context.

Once a manuscript is under review, authors cannot change it unless the journal sends it back, and journals did not then check references for retractions as they do now; so he says authors cannot find such references unless the journal checks them and asks for a correction, and that such citations are inevitable in reviews with hundreds of references that pass through several journals. He says the retracted references, 11 of the 1,546 in the seven reviews, have no significant negative effect on the reviews' topics or conclusions. He also said the first item, Roberts JT et al. (Ann Oncol 2006), is not retracted and has no retraction notice.

replies.summary: Dr Bernad says the 2005 paper was the first report of an apparent spontaneous transformation of mesenchymal stem cells in culture, at a time when these cells were being tested in many cell therapies, so it had a large impact on the field. Soon after publication his group found that the main conclusion could not be reproduced and was most probably due to a very small number of contaminating transformed cells that overgrew the cultures. He says the group contacted Cancer Research to offer a retraction; the journal preferred a short notice (de la Fuente et al., 2010) to the longer one they wrote. He says the group approached the journal soon after finding the result could not be reproduced. He did not give the date of that contact by 28 October (the notice was published in August 2010). He proposed a note for later authors, printed below as he wrote it, and points to his group's later work on long-term culture of these cells.
replies.quote: Soon after publication (Rubio et al., 2005) we realized that the main conclusion was non reproducible and that the putative spontaneous transformation was most probably due to a highly minoritarian number of a transformed cell line.
replies.statement: Please, be aware that the main conclusion of the manuscript (Rubio et al., 2005) was non-reproducible and that the putative spontaneous transformation of MSC, upon in vitro culture, was most probably due to a highly minoritarian number of contaminant- transformed cells, that with time overgrow the cultures. Then it was retracted (de la Fuente et al., 2010). Therefore, continue citing this work as a proof of the potential of MSC to be transformed upon prolonged in vitro culture, is no appropriate and can induce more confusion to the field
replies.our_response: The retraction notice was published in Cancer Research in August 2010 (doi:10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-10-2451). His group's later papers: Estrada JC et al., Cell Death Dis 2013 (replicative senescence of these cells in long-term culture is closely linked to aneuploidy) and Sepúlveda JC et al., Stem Cells 2014 (senescence abrogates their therapeutic potential in a mouse model of lethal endotoxemia). The entry stands: the citations counted were made after the retraction and use the paper as support.
changes: Reason changed from the Retraction Watch group "error or unreliable results" to the notice's wording: the authors could not reproduce some of the transformation events and suspect a cross-contamination artifact; five of the seven authors agreed to the retraction.
